question: How does replacing 5%, 10%, and 15% of natural sand with crushed tire rubber affect the compressive strength of high-performance concrete compared to regular concrete?
answer: The strength of the concrete decreased by 14%, 28%, and 51% when replacing 5%, 10%, and 15% of the sand with rubber, respectively.
text:
## Results and discussion

Using different types of crushed tire rubber instead of natural sand had clear effects on the properties of the concrete. The concrete's workability, hardness over time, and response to movement were all considered. When the rubber was mixed into the concrete, there was a slight decrease in its ability to flow, known as "slump." This was due to the shape and surface of the rubber pieces. Despite this, the concrete performed well for regular building and compacting. The weight of the concrete also decreased by about 2% when using 15% rubber because rubber pieces are lighter than natural sand. After the concrete had time to harden, its strength and flexibility were tested. Compared to regular concrete, the strength decreased by 14%, 28%, and 51% when replacing 5%, 10%, and 15% of the sand with rubber. However, all mixtures retained enough strength for many uses. The flexibility of the concrete also decreased, especially with 15% rubber. The concrete's response to the movement was examined. With 15% rubber, it was a bit less rigid but better at resisting vibrations. Examining the concrete's structure, changes were observed around the rubber particles. Using crushed tire rubber in concrete instead of sand can improve its ability to absorb vibrations while maintaining sufficient strength, especially with less than 10% rubber. Choosing smaller rubber pieces helps preserve workability and strength. With the right mix and treatment, this method could be valuable for recycling old tires in constructing robust structures.

These results provide insights into the performance characteristics of each mix in comparison to the control mix (M1), which serves as a benchmark for evaluating the viability of alternative materials. The conventional M1 mix achieved compressive strengths of 37.25 MPa at 7 days, 46.74 MPa at 28 days, and 51.31 MPa at 90 days, demonstrating consistent performance and establishing a reference for assessing the effects of material substitutions. The 10% fly ash mix (M5) exhibited compressive strengths of 35.61 MPa at 7 days, 45.09 MPa at 28 days, and 45.55 MPa at 90 days. While slightly lower than the control mix at early curing stages, the results highlight the pozzolanic activity of fly ash, which enhances longterm strength development. The delayed strength gain is attributed to the slow hydration process of fly ash, forming additional cementitious compounds over time. question: What temperature and duration were used to burn pulverized coconut shell into char and ash, and what was the approximate percentage reduction in weight after this process?
answer: The pulverized coconut shell was burnt at a temperature of 800 degrees for 2 hours, resulting in a weight reduction of about 40%.
text: Coconut shell, an agricultural waste, was cleaned and air-dried under the sun for 6 hours to remove moisture. The sample was pulverized and burnt into char and ashes at a temperature of 800 degrees for 2 hours. The weight of the coconut shell was reduced by about 40% after burning. It was further milled into particles and sieved using a 75μm sieve to obtain the coconut shell ash for the experiment [1]. Concrete mix design was developed to guide the process (see Table 1). A trial mix design method, targeting a mean strength, was employed. Firstly, the control concrete, which had 0% CSA, was prepared to achieve the targeted compressive strength of 20 N/mm 2 at 28 days of curing. In the design, the water-to-cement ratio was selected as 0.59. Then, PLC was partially replaced with CSA in proportions of 5%, 10%, 15% and 20%. Concrete mixes were named as CSA 0, CSA 5, CSA 10, CSA 15, and CSA 20, when CSA partially replaced cement (PLC) in proportions of 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20%, respectively. The 150mm x 150mm x 150mm concrete molds were used. Three concrete specimens were tested at ages 7 days, 28 days, 70 days for compressive strength following BS EN 12390-3:2019 [14], density of concrete was determined in accordance with BS EN 12390-7:2009 [15], water absorption test of concrete in accordance with BS EN 1881-122: 2011 [16], and flexural strength following BS EN 12390-5: 2019 [17]. Concrete was mixed and cured in accordance with BS EN 12390-2, 2000 [18]. The grading test for coarse aggregates for the concrete mix followed the procedures outlined in BS EN 933-1:2012 [13], which specify the sieving method for determining aggregate size [13]. The sieves used were: 22mm, 20mm, 19mm, 14mm, 12.5mm, 10mm, 4.75mm, and 2.36mm. Grading test for fine aggregate (sand) for concrete was done in accordance with BS EN 933-1:2012 [13], and classified following BS 882:1992 and BS EN 12620:2013 [19, 20]. The specific sieves used for the test were: 5mm, 4.75mm, 2.36mm, 1.18mm, 0.6mm, 0.3mm, 0.15mm, and 0.075mm.

question: How does the acid exposure resistance of the type-3 concrete mixture containing metakaolin compare to the control mix, and what specific chemical mechanisms are cited to explain this enhanced performance?
answer: The type-3 mixture exhibits 53% higher resistance than the control mix. This is attributed to metakaolin consuming calcium hydroxide via a pozzolanic reaction, which reduces the formation of expansive gypsum and fills capillary gaps with secondary C-S-H gel, thereby reducing overall permeability.
text:
Figure 10 shows the performance against the acid exposure for all three types of mixtures as the percentages of foundry sand increase. The test is carried out in accordance to ASTM C267 standrad. The type-1 mix containing fly ash exhibited 40% higher resistance than the control mix (without supplementary cementitious material), with 20% foundry sand. The high strength and density of the material can be due to the pozzolanic features of fly ash, which promote the formation of a significant amount of C-S-H gel 49 . The type-2 mix, including silica fume, exhibits a 45% greater resistance than the control mix. The enhanced performance of this material is attributed to the characteristic of silica fume, which enhances the adhesive strength between the aggregate and paste, decreases the calcium content, and reduces the concrete porosity; as a result, concrete becomes more impermeable and durable 48,56-58 . Furthermore, in the case of the type-3 mix, the resistance is 53% more than the control mix. When MK replaces some of the Portland cement in a mixture, less tricalcium aluminate hydrate is required to create the cement paste matrix. The second process involves consuming some of the calcium hydroxides produced during cement hydration via a pozzolanic reaction involving the MK and the calcium hydroxide. As a result, MK concrete will have less of the expansive gypsum produced by the reactivity of calcium hydroxide than ordinary concrete. Although the pozzolanic reaction's secondary C-S-H is less thick than the original C-S-H gel, it does a good job of filling and segmenting otherwise enormous capillary gaps into smaller, discontinuous ones. As a result, concrete loses some of its permeability overall 47,59 . The descriptive statistics are shown in Table 10.

question: How does the incorporation of silica fume and the level of coconut shell replacement respectively affect the water absorption and effective porosity of coconut shell-silica fume (CS-SF) concrete?
answer: The incorporation of silica fume reduces water absorption and effective porosity due to pozzolanic activity and the creation of extra C-S-H gel, which refines the pore structure. Conversely, higher levels of coconut shell replacement increase water absorption and effective porosity owing to the inherent porous character of the shell aggregates.
text:
Figure 4 shows Percentage change of water absorption (%) of coconut shell-silica fume (CS-SF) concrete after 28, 56 and 90 days. The 28days, 56days, and 90days curing periods are indicated by blue, orange and gray bars respectively. The progressive refinement of the pores and the densification of the matrix as a result of the continued hydration and pozzolanic activity of silica fume is supported by a decreasing trend with curing age. The error bars signify ±1 standard deviation of three specimens. The bar graph shows how the water absorption varies with the age of curing. The trend of all mixes shows a decreasing pattern between 28 days and 90 days, which suggests progressive hydration and pore refinement. The pozzolanic reaction and the creation of extra C-S-H gel of silica fume resulted in the reduction of water absorption when compared to the control mix. But mixtures with a better percentage of coconut shells gave a higher absorption value due to the inherent porous character of the shell aggregates.

Figure 5 shows Effective porosity (%) of 28, 56 and 90days control and CS-SF concrete mixes. The decrease of porosity with the age of curing implies microstructural refinements. The porous nature of shell aggregates is what increases the porosity at larger levels of coconut shell replacement. The error bars signify ±1 standard deviation of three specimens. The effective porosity results show a progressive decrease with the age of curing, which is an indication of the densification of the cement matrix. Incorporation of silica fume results in microstructural refinement of secondary hydration, which decreases the pore connectivity. On the other hand, increased degree of coconut shell replacement enhanced overall porosity owing to the porous and light weight shell aggregates. The variation of water absorption of the CS-SF concrete mixes at different curing ages (28, 56, and 90 days) is summarized in Table 8. Table 9 shows the values of effective porosity of the concrete mixes at various curing ages, which demonstrates the impact of silica fume and replacement by coconut shell on the development of pore structure.

For all durability tests (Tables 8-13), the reported values represent the average of 28, 56, and 90 days. The standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (COV) were calculated based on replicate 90days measurements. It is found that the higher the CS content the greater the water absorption due to increasing pore connectivity and decreasing interfacial transition zones (ITZ), which enhance capillary movement.

question: How does the reduction in montmorillonite-related peaks in marine clay treated with lime, POFA, and calcined shale contribute to the material's stability and plasticity?
answer: The reduction in montmorillonite peaks suggests that the additives improve the clay structure, resulting in better stability and reduced plasticity, because montmorillonite is an expansive clay mineral that causes high swelling and moisture sensitivity.
text: The XRD patterns in Figure 19 clearly show the mineralogical variations that occurred after treating marine clay with Lime, POFA, and CS over 90 curing days. The untreated sample shows sharp and strong diffraction peaks, particularly the dominant quartz around 26° 2θ. In addition, small peaks of kaolinite and montmorillonite. These pronounced peaks confirm the highly crystalline composition of the original soil minerals and indicate the relatively low reactivity of the untreated marine clay structure. In contrast, the S+3%L+5%POFA+10%CS sample exhibited a clear decrease in quartz peak intensity along with the emergence of several CSH peaks. The reduction or disappearance of the montmorillonite and kaolin peaks can be attributed to their inherently low intensity, whereas the decrease in the quartz peak is likely due to the formation of cementitious products throughout the curing period [59]. Another notable observation is that the peaks in treated samples became broader and less intense compared to those of the untreated sample around 2θ values of 26°, 27°, 37°, and 50°. This change indicates a reduction in crystallinity, suggesting that part of the crystalline clay minerals transformed into amorphous phases are commonly associated with successful soil stabilization, as they help enhance strength and improve the long-term durability. The identification of hydrated states via X-ray diffraction (XRD) is challenging due to the amorphous nature of CSH gels [60]. These hydrates typically manifest as broad humps around 2θ values of 29.5°, 32°, 37°, and 50°, as reported by Kulasuriya et al. [61]. The reduction in montmorillonite-related peaks is also significant, which enhances the treated samples, as Montmorillonite is an expansive clay mineral that causes high swelling and moisture sensitivity in marine clay. Its partial reduction during stabilization suggests that the additives improve the clay structure, resulting in better stability and reduced plasticity. Table 10 provides the X-ray fluorescence (XRF) results. The presence and variations in the percentages of SiO ₂ , Al ₂ O ₃ , and other elements in the treated samples with POFA, lime, and CS confirm the formation of cementitious compounds.

question: What mechanism explains the reduction in the modulus of elasticity of copper slag-based geopolymer concrete when the copper slag replacement level exceeds 40%?
answer: The reduction is attributed to excess slag particles overwhelming the available binder, which leads to inadequate coating of aggregates and poor bonding at the interfacial transition zone (ITZ). Additionally, further increasing the copper slag content reduces mix homogeneity and increases the risk of microcracks due to brittleness, thereby lowering the elastic stiffness of the composite.
text:
MOE of 70% fly ash and 30% GGBS with 40% slag replaced as a fine aggregate shows higher MOE of about 3.67x10 4 MPa, 3.71x10 4 MPa and 3.92x10 4 MPa at 8M, 10M and 12M respectively. Beyond the 40% replacement of FA with slag there is a reduction in the MOE is observed. The enhancement in the MOE is attributed to the filler effect of slag particles and matrix densification. The angular shape and rough surface of CS enhance the interfacial bond between the aggregate and the geopolymer matrix, reduces porosity and improves stiffness. Beyond 40%, MOE value reduction attributed to the excess slag particles overwhelming the available binder, leading to inadequate coating of aggregates and poor bonding at the interfacial transition zone (ITZ). Further increasing CS content, reduces the homogeneity of the mix and increases the risk of microcracks due to brittleness, thereby lowering the elastic stiffness of the composite.

Fig 7. MOEand Percentage variation in strength with respect to molarity

Anincreasing trend in the MOE is observed in all molarity levels from the mix CS 0 to CS 40, beyond 40% reduction in MOE is observed in all the molarity levels. Among the mixes, CS40 demonstrates the highest improvement in MOE across all molarity levels, indicating that 40% copper slag replacement is the optimum proportion. MOE of GPC mix CS 40 is increased about 30.14%, 19.29% and 25.24% at 8M, 10M and 12M respectively compared to the control mix CS 0. Beyond 40% replacement, the excess CS content reduces workability and leads to insufficient binder coating on aggregate particles. This weakens the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), creates heterogeneity, and increases microcrack formation, ultimately causing a decline in MOE at higher replacement levels.

Research findings on the elastic modulus of concrete incorporating copper slag (CS) show mixed trends. Several studies report that CS concrete exhibits an elastic modulus similar to that of control mixes, with some indicating a slight improvement depending on the replacement level. The increase in modulus has also been linked to its correlation with compressive strength. Conversely, other studies have observed a marginal decrease in elastic modulus when CS is used, which has been attributed to the presence of impurities in the slag. Overall, the influence of CS on elastic modulus is not consistent, showing both minor gains andslight reductions depending on mix proportions and material characteristics (12) . question: What is the proposed explanation for the observed workability in silica fume-modified coconut shell aggregate concrete mixes, and how does the highest silica fume blend (10%) compare to conventional concrete in terms of slump?
answer: The workability is explained by a decrease in the amount of water required due to the low porosity of the concrete matrix. The highest silica fume blend at 10% registered a slump of 79 mm, which is lower than the 89 mm slump obtained for conventional concrete.
text:
Table 11 shows Slump values of Conventional and Coconut Shell Concrete mixtures. Generally, adding of mineral based admixtures reduces the workability of concrete because the mineral admixtures are more water absorbent. In this experiment, the slump obtained with the conventional concrete (CC) was 89 mm and mixes that used silica fume had slump values that ranged between 69 mm and 81 mm. The lightweight aggregate (LWA) concrete slump values of 50-70 mm are compared to the normal weight concrete (NWC) slump values of 100-125 mm according to (Mehta and Monteiro, 2014). The concrete mixes that used silica fume were identified to be in the category of highly workable mixes. The highest silica fume blend at 10 percent registered the highest slump of 79 mm. There was no evidence of segregation in all the silica fume concrete mixes. This enhancement of its workability can be probably explained by the decrease in the amount of water required which is caused by the low porosity of the concrete matrix. Figure 3 shows the behaviour of slump with various levels of silica fume. Sustainable lightweight concretes have also been observed to be affected by silica fume, where the ultra-fine size of particles affects the workability because of improved paste cohesion and decreased bleeding (Kumar et al., 2022) found out that SCMs especially silica fume decreases slump but increases the stability of lightweight concrete mixtures. Equally, Vargas et al. (2024) noted with the help of ensemble ML modelling that workability parameters (slump) can be reasonably predicted with variations of binder and water-cement ratios, showing that the mentioned relationships possess nonlinear trends that are consistent with the results of this study.

## 4.1.1 XRD pattern of cement

Mineral phases in the XRD test have shown that there are a number of significant crystalline phases which produce different contribution to the properties and behaviour of the material. Key elements that were found to be hematite, calcite, alumina, and quartz. The hematite is present as shown by the separate peaks in the XRD pattern. Hematite is one of the types of common impurities of iron oxide in cement that could be a product of raw materials like iron ore used in manufacturing it. It has the potential to affect the cement colour and bring about slight strengthening impacts. The calcite diffraction peaks indicate either the material has not been fully reacted or that there has been subsequent carbonation of the material that could have occurred during transportation or storage. This calcite may be used as a micro-filler and can be used to augment the density of the hardened matrix in terms of particle packing though with insignificant effect on strength. Peaks based on alumina indicate the presence of aluminous compounds which are important in the first hydration process. The hydration products that were detected are calcium aluminate hydrates which determine setting properties and early strength. The XRD pattern was analysed, which revealed quartz as a result of its distinctive peaks. This shows that there was some silica remaining in the raw materials. Even though, the quartz does not take part in the hydration of the cement, it is an inert filler that would promote the stability of the cement matrix. Figure 4 represents the XRD pattern of cement. The crystal phases identified are in line with the previous studies that show existence of active and non-active mineral constituents in cementitious materials. A comparison of OPC systems based on close XRD spectra in Li et al. (2023) showed that the existence of calcite and quartz are stable fillers that did not affect the kinetics of hydration significantly, yet enhanced dimensional stability. The unique phase determination ensures reasonable chemical modelling and data integrity of the dataset used in the subsequent modelling analysis.

question: What factors are attributed to the reduction in compressive strength when increasing the content of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and palm kernel shell (PKS) in concrete?
answer: The reduction is attributed to the smooth and hydrophobic surface of PET particles weakening the bond with cement paste, the porous and lightweight nature of PKS aggregates leading to higher void content and lower density, and the inclusion of these materials reducing workability and compaction quality, which increases internal air voids.

As shown in Table 6, the 7-day compressive strength test conducted at the Civil Engineering Laboratory of Universitas Muhammadiyah Tangerang yielded the highest value for the control sample (PET 0% - PKS 0%), which achieved a maximum load of 190,000 N and a compressive strength of 10.76 MPa. The concrete with 1% PET - 10% PKS substitution recorded a lower compressive strength of 7.93 MPa, while the 2% PET - 20% PKS mixture showed the lowest strength of 7.36 MPa, corresponding to maximum loads of 140,000 N and 130,000 N, respectively.

The reduction in compressive strength with increasing PET and PKS content can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, the smooth and hydrophobic surface of PET particles weakens the bond between the plastic and the cement paste, resulting in poor interfacial adhesion and reduced load transfer efficiency. Secondly, the porous and lightweight nature of PKS aggregates leads to higher void content and lower density in the hardened concrete, which diminishes its overall compressive capacity. Additionally, the inclusion of these waste materials tends to reduce the workability and compaction quality of the concrete mix, increasing internal air voids that further decrease strength.

Overall, the results indicate that the incorporation of PET and PKS waste beyond small proportions adversely affects the microstructure of concrete. Nevertheless, limited substitution levels (around 1% PET and 10% PKS) may still be utilized for non-structural applications, promoting material sustainability without excessively compromising mechanical performance.

question: What factors are primarily attributed to the reduction in workability observed in geopolymer concrete mixtures with high sugarcane bagasse ash (SCBA) content and higher NaOH molarity?
answer: The reduction in workability is primarily attributed to the high specific surface area and elevated liquid absorption capacity of the SCBA particles, increased adsorption of the alkaline solution and superplasticizer by the residual carbonaceous fraction due to high LOI, and the increased viscosity of higher molarity alkaline solutions which accelerates geopolymerization kinetics.
text:

All analyses were conducted at the National Research Centre, Giza, Egypt. A Tescan VEGA3 scanning electron microscope was used for the SEM/ EDX investigation. The morphology and elemental composition of dried, gold-coated fragments obtained from crushed concrete specimens were systematically examined. SEM/EDX and XRD analyses were performed on selected representative mixtures rather than all fifteen investigated mixtures. The selected specimens were chosen to represent the principal variables of the experimental program, including the control mixture, the B25 mixture, higher SCBA contents, different NaOH molarities, and selected elevated-temperature exposure conditions., different NaOH molarities, and selected elevated-temperature exposure conditions. This representative selection was intended to identify the microstructural changes associated with the investigated variables and to provide representative evidence supporting the trends observed in the mechanical, durability, and thermal performance results. Because only selected specimens were examined, the microstructural observations should be interpreted as representative evidence and should not be generalized to all fifteen mixtures without further characterization.

Notably, the B25 mixture (containing 25% SCBA and prepared with 14 M NaOH) exhibited a slump of 90 mm, demonstrating satisfactory and promising workability for practical applications. Conversely, a sharp decline in flowability was observed at higher replacement levels (75% and 95% SCBA), where slump values dropped below 70 mm and 55 mm, respectively, regardless of the NaOH concentration. This reduction in workability is primarily attributed to the high specific surface area and elevated liquid absorption capacity of the SCBA particles. The high LOI of the SCBA may have additionally contributed to this behavior through increased adsorption of the alkaline solution and superplasticizer by the residual carbonaceous fraction. Furthermore, the higher molarity of the alkaline solution increases its viscosity, which subsequently accelerates the geopolymerization kinetics and impedes mixture flowability. The total embodied energy per unit volume for each mixture was calculated using Equation (5).

However, at 75% replacement, the density declined to values close to or below the control. This reduction indicates that excessive use of ceramic tiles disrupts the aggregate skeleton, increases voids, and lowers compactness. question: What mechanism explains the increase in compressive strength of palm kernel shell ash (PKSA) blended cement concrete at later ages (60 and 90 days) compared to early ages, specifically regarding the role of PKSA?
answer: At later ages, PKSA exhibits pozzolanic characteristics by reacting with the free lime (Ca(OH)2) released during cement hydration to generate additional calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) and hydrated calcium aluminates. This process enhances interfacial bonding between the aggregates and pastes, leading to an improvement in compressive strength.
text:
The trend of the CF in Figure 4 indicated a reduction in the workability of the concrete mix with an increase in pozzolan content. The compacting factor values for 0.65 - ratio which was used for the mix design is considered as satisfactory as it falls within low to medium workability for control to 30% dosage of PKSA. Precisely, the compacting Factor assesses the impact of a standard amount of work (height of fall) on compaction, and necessitates sufficient water content to attain relatively complete compaction. This is true in the case of water-binder ratio of 0.65 used for all the mixes.

## Compressive strength test

The strength development rate is primarily dependent on the hydration rate of cement influenced by both the initial hydration of palm kernel shell ash and subsequent rehydration due to pozzolanic reactivity of PKSA in the concrete blend of PKSA/OPC. At the early ages of 3, 7, 14 and 28 days, the trend was a reduction in compressive strength as the volume of PKSA increased from 5% to 30% replacement in comparison to the control concrete. This phenomenon could be ascribed to the dilution effect and delayed initiation of the pozzolanic reaction of Ca(OH)2 in the PKSA. At the later ages of 60- and 90-days hydration the strengths tended to be constant from control to 10% except at 15% replacement which gave strengths slightly higher than the control concrete. Indeed, this aligns with the observation that the strength of pozzolanic materials rises as the hydration of the cementitious materials increases, driven by the reaction between free lime released during cement hydration and the silica content of supplementary cementitious materials (SCM). Therefore, at this later stage, the amorphous aluminous and siliceous minerals could still be actively reacting with Ca(OH)2, generating additional C-S-H and hydrated calcium aluminates. This process enhances interfacial bonding between the aggregates and pastes leading to an improvement in the compressive strength of concrete.

While as the age of curing increased from 3 days to 90 days despite the increase in PKSA content a gradual increase in compressive strength development was observed. This suggests that PKSA has the potential to contribute to latestage strength development. The lower compressive strength of the concrete at early ages could be attributed to the fact that, in the initial stages of hydration the PKSA pozzolan may have acted as a filler, occupying voids between paste and sand. As time progresses it transforms into a pozzolan, influencing its pozzolanic action on the concrete by converting excess Ca(OH)2 into useful C-S-H which is crucial for strength gain. This behavior indicates that PKSA exhibits pozzolanic characteristics.

question: Why is the coefficient of variation for splitting tensile strength notably higher than that for compressive strength and elastic modulus in limestone calcined clay cement-based recycled aggregate concrete?
answer: The higher coefficient of variation for splitting tensile strength is likely due to the impact of randomly distributed microcracks and pores on the tensile crack path.
text:
Figure 4a also shows how different variables affect the variation in compressive strength. As the water-tobinder ratio, RA content or combined use of metakaolin and limestone powder increased, the compressive strength variation generally increased. Among the 18 concrete mixes in Table 1, M15 had the lowest compressive strength variation at 4.70%, while M9 had the highest at 7.94%, a difference of 3.24%. This highlights that using recycled or substitute materials may lead to instability in concrete performance, a point that requires attention from experts.

Figure 4c presents the statistical characteristics of the splitting tensile strength for the 18 concrete types. Key observations were as follows: (i) The coefficient of variation for splitting tensile strength was notably higher than for compressive strength and elastic modulus, likely due to the impact of randomly distributed microcracks and pores on the tensile crack path 29 . (ii) Similar to elastic modulus, splitting tensile strength increased with a decrease in water-to-binder ratio, though the increase was smaller than in compressive strength. Additionally, LC3-based RAC exhibited less variation in splitting tensile strength for the same change in water-to-binder ratio. (iii) Replacing cement with metakaolin and limestone powder reduced splitting tensile strength, with the effect becoming more pronounced at substitution rates above 30%. At 50% and 70% substitution, the 28-day tensile strength decreased by 6.4% and 10.1%, respectively. (iv) The content and quality of RAs significantly influenced splitting tensile strength. For instance, as the volume replacement rate of fine RAs increased from 0 to 60%, the tensile strength dropped by 47.9%. When the compressive strength of the parent concrete decreased from 45.6 to 21.5 MPa, splitting tensile strength decreased by 15.2%. (v) An increase in water-to-binder ratio, higher use of metakaolin and limestone powder, and the addition of RAs all increased the variability of the splitting tensile strength.

answer: Laterite has a lower coefficient of uniformity (Cu) of 3.20 compared to 4.88 for sand, indicating a narrower range of particle sizes that reduces its ability to fill voids effectively. text:
Similarly, at equal PKS levels, increasing laterite content raises ISAT 10 values, as its finer claylike particles and higher water demand contribute to interparticle voids and reduced packing efficiency.

At a 0.4 water-cement ratio, ISAT 10 values (×10⁻² ml/m²s) at 20% PKS replacement increased from 52 (10% laterite) to 55 (20% laterite) and further to 58 (30% laterite) after 28 days. Sieve analysis results further explain this behavior. Laterite is poorly graded compared to sand, as indicated by its lower coefficient of uniformity (Cu), which is 3.20 compared to 4.88 for sand. This narrower range of particle sizes in laterite reduces its ability to fill voids effectively. Similarly, the coefficient of curvature (Cc) for laterite is 0.94, slightly higher than sand's 0.92, but still below the ideal range of 1 - 3, indicating an imbalance in the distribution of intermediate-sized particles.

(Yuan et al. 2023) demonstrated that fibres improved freeze-thaw resistance under sulphate attack. The fibre reinforcement helps maintain the integrity of concrete, ensuring it is more resilient in the presence of freeze-thaw cycles and sulphate exposure. Moreover, fibres provided excellent protection against wet-dry cycles and chloride exposure, with only superficial rust visible on the fibres after exposure (Â. Graeff 2011). ## 6. Environmental analysis and material performance

## 6.1. Energy Consumption Metrics

Energy consumption represents an essential dimension of environmental performance in evaluating fibre-reinforced and 3DPC. Thermal efficiency is one important consideration which affects operational energy use over a building's lifecycle. For instance, studies reported a 62% reduction in thermal conductivity when expanded perlite aggregate was incorporated into concrete mixes (Malek et al. 2020; Mustafa et al. 2022). This improved insulation potential reduces energy demands for heating and cooling, lowering overall energy consumption in building operations. However, the energy demands during production must also be addressed. (Jones & Li 2023) observed that normal strength 3DPC, while yielding a 23% reduction in CO2 emissions, required 29% more energy during production than traditional methods. (Chaofan et al. 2023; Kailun et al. 2024) noted that geopolymer-based 3DPC consumes less energy than conventional cement-based alternatives, reinforcing the environmental advantages of alkali-activated binder systems. (Rajeev et al. 2023) showed that using recycled face mask fibres enhanced the insulation performance of concrete, indirectly reducing energy needs over the service life of the building.

question: How do lower prediction errors in the predictive models for fiber-reinforced rubberized recycled aggregate concrete (FRRAC) enhance mix design and structural safety?
answer: Lower prediction errors enhance mix design by reducing overdesign, saving materials, and lowering embodied carbon while maintaining reliability. They also enable more precise safety margins, support better partial factor decisions, and avoid under- or overestimation of structural capacity.
text:
Regarding the developed study, some limitations and the most related suggestions could be recognized as follows. The 102 samples that make up the study's small dataset might restrict how far the findings can be applied. Therefore, increase the dataset's size by gathering additional samples from various resources to boost the dependability and robustness of the model. When paired with methodologies such as 𝐶ℎ𝑂𝐴 and 𝐴𝑅𝑂𝐴 , the 𝐿𝑆𝑆𝑉𝑅 model may be computationally demanding, which presents issues for scalability and real-time applications. To fix this and make the model more useful for real-world applications, investigate ways to maximise computational efficiency, such as more effective computing approaches or streamlined methods. The research concentrates on certain kinds of recycled materials ( 𝑅𝐶𝐴 and 𝐶𝑅 ) with defined qualities; hence, variations in the composition and quality of these materials frcom other resources might impact the precision of the model. To further improve the model's comprehensiveness and flexibility, include a greater variety of input parameters, such as additives, ambient conditions, and fibre kinds. The lack of external datasets from various geographic regions or climatic conditions to evaluate the models may have compromised the applicability of the results. Additionally, to assess the models' precision and practical applicability, conduct real-world testing and validate them utilizing external datasets from diverse places and situations. Through empirical research and long-term monitoring, examine the long-term performance and stability of 𝐹𝑅𝑅𝐴𝐶 as anticipated by these models. To promote sustainable practices, carry out a thorough study of the environmental effect. Enhancing the predictive modelling of flexural strength in 𝐹𝑅𝑅𝐴𝐶 may lead to more sustainable and effective building methods by resolving these constraints and putting the relevant suggestions into practice.

Turning to the practical applications, the predictive models enable engineers to create 𝐹𝑅𝑅𝐴𝐶 mixes with the appropriate flexural strength, guaranteeing that the finished concrete satisfies certain structural specifications. Customized concrete formulas that strike a balance between performance, affordability, and sustainability are made possible by this. Also, before concrete is utilized in structural applications, construction firms may use these models to estimate and confirm the material's flexural strength as part of their quality control procedures. Moreover, by ensuring that only concrete with sufficient strength is used, structures and infrastructure will be safer and more resilient. The building industry may save waste and lessen its need on natural aggregates by adding recycled materials like 𝑅𝐶𝐴 and CR to concrete. Interestingly, the use of predictive models guarantees that the structural integrity of the concrete is not jeopardised by the use of sustainable materials. By experimenting with various ratios of recycled materials and additions, researchers may quickly design new, more environmentally friendly concrete compositions by using these models. Furthermore, the models may be utilized to evaluate and forecast how well 𝐹𝑅𝑅𝐴𝐶 will work in the rehabilitation of already-existing buildings, especially when it comes to fixing or strengthening ageing infrastructure. These models provide useful insights into the application of machine learning in building material science, making them useful teaching aids for students studying civil engineering. These results have direct engineering implications for FRRAC beyond numerical advantages. Lower prediction errors enhance mix design by reducing overdesign, saving materials, and lowering embodied carbon while maintaining reliability. They enable more precise safety margins, support better partial factor decisions, and avoid under- or overestimation. Improved accuracy reduces lab iterations, shortens development cycles, cuts testing costs, and helps acceptance tests with fewer re-tests. Better strength predictions optimize fiber dosage, meeting performance needs without extra costs or workability issues. For asset management, sharper flexural capacity estimates prioritize interventions and justify approvals. To ensure comparability, we retain PI and other indices and will include MAPE in future work for comprehensive assessment.

In the Discussion, we also examine the study's limitations and suggest directions for future research, summarized below.

question: How does the addition of granite industrial waste (GW) affect the mass loss of self-compacting sand concrete (SCSC) mixtures at 800°C, and what mechanism explains this reduction?
answer: The addition of GW decreased the mass loss of SCSC mixtures at 800°C, reducing it from 7.95% in the control mixture to 5.77%, 6.52%, and 7.02% for the 5SSP + 40GW, 10SSP + 40GW, and 15SSP + 40GW mixtures, respectively. This reduction is attributed to improved bonding between the angular, rough-surfaced GW particles and the cement paste in the interfacial transition zone, which limits water expulsion and reduces thermal deterioration.
text:
Figure 16 shows the impact of high temperature on mass loss in SCSC specimens. The results clearly reveal that increasing temperature led to higher mass loss in all SCSC mixtures. This increase in mass loss at elevated temperatures can be explained by the evaporation of capillary water and the decomposition of C-S-H gel and CaCO₃ [49]. The heat generated within the SCSC causes pore pressure, which directly induces spalling, especially at 800°C, as shown in Fig. 18. It was observed that the mass loss values of SCSC mixtures containing 5%, 10%, and 15% SSP without GW (5SSP + 0GW, 10SSP + 0GW, and 15SSP + 0GW) were higher than those of the control SCSC mixture in the temperature range of 200-800°C. This is attributed to the decomposition of seashells at high temperatures, which creates pores in the matrix. These pores contribute to crack patterns and facilitate heat dissipation [50]. In addition, 5SSP + 0GW had fewer pores than 10SSP + 0GW and 15SSP + 0GW and was unable to dissipate pore pressure effectively, which led to spalling at 800°C (Fig. 18).

Furthermore, the addition of GW decreased the mass loss of SCSC mixtures, from 7.95% for the control SCSC to 5.77%, 6.52%, and 7.02% for 5SSP + 40GW, 10SSP + 40GW, and 15SSP + 40GW mixtures, respectively. These values are 27.42%, 17.98%, and 11.69% lower than the control SCSC mixture at 800°C. This reduction can be attributed to improved bonding between GW aggregates and cement paste in the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), due to the angular shape and rough surface of GW particles (Fig. 2b), as confirmed by the flexural strength results (3.2.2). This stronger bonding limits water expulsion and reduces the thermal deterioration of the concrete structure [51,52]. Jain et al. [53] also reported about 6% weight loss when substituting around 60% of fine aggregate with GW in SCC exposed to fire up to 800°C.

question: What specific advantage does waste foundry sand (WFS) offer over other industrial byproducts like copper slag and steel slag that makes it suitable for environmentally friendly concrete production?
answer: WFS is free of harmful elements, whereas copper slag and steel slag comprise heavy metals and other toxic elements.
text:
The use of waste foundry sand (WFS) in the production of concrete is a potential replacement for natural sand because it has the most advantages in terms of being an industrial raw material compared to other industrial byproducts.WFS possesses high silica sand and there is a large availability of it at very low cost, which makes it a best material for high volume concrete production. WFS is free of harmful elements compared to the other industrial by-products like copper slag and steel slag which comprises heavy metals and other toxic elements, making WFS environment friendly for construction. In addition to this advantage, WFS was found to enhance the mechanical properties of concrete, including tensile and compressive strength, which reveals the potential uses of WFS for environmentally friendly concrete production 8-10 . The chosen values for percentage replacements of waste foundry sand (WFS) in concrete mixes were 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% which were derived as a combination of preliminary studies and literature benchmarks. Previous studies showed that a small percentage of WFS (5-10%) display a considerable enhancement in concrete properties while maintaining acceptable workability and durability in concrete 7,44 . The following dosage rates for fly ash, metakaolin, and silica fume were examined in this study, based on the literature survey, properties of materials and initial trial mixtures. The materials used in this work were ordinary Portland cement, fly ash replacing at a rate of 50 kg/m³ which provides an economical and durability solutions 45,46 , metakaolin at a percentage of 10% because of its early strength 33,47 , and silica fume at 5% of the total volume due to bonding and compressive strength enhancement 48,49 .These rates were established by trial mixes to attain desirable workability, strength and durability with regard to test groups.

question: How does the Random Forest algorithm mitigate overfitting and increase robustness through its bagging mechanism and feature selection strategy?
answer: Random Forest mitigates overfitting by training multiple decision trees on different bootstrapped subsets of the dataset and combining their predictions, which reduces variance. Additionally, by allowing only a randomized subset of input features at each splitting node, the algorithm ensures increased diversity and prevents overdependence on specific features, thereby improving generalization to unseen data.
text:
RF is a strong ensemble learning algorithm, applicable to both classification and regression problems. The approach is based on bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating), which means multiple decision trees are trained on different subsets of the dataset, and the predictions of the decision trees are combined to increase accuracy and avoid overfitting. This way, RF becomes more robust by reducing variance and generalizing to unseen data.

Each decision tree within the forest is trained on the bootstrapped sample drawn from the same source dataset that included some duplicated observations. Second, at the splitting node within each tree, only a randomized subset of input features is allowed, rather than processing all features every time, ensuring increased diversity and no overdependence on certain selected features. Combining the class or regression scores for individual decision trees gives us the final predicted score for class classification and means regression.

question: What is the primary mechanism attributed to the gain in compressive strength observed in high volume fly ash concrete mixes at later ages, and what specific chemical reaction occurs?
answer: The strength gain is attributed to the densification of the microstructure resulting from the Pozzolanic Reaction, which involves the reaction between reactive silica and alumina constituents of fly ash with Portlandite to form secondary C-S-H and sometimes C-A-S-H.
text: On the perusal of the test results, it was observed that effect of water-binder ratio along with flyash content had a significant influence over strength value. From the figure 2 to 3, it can be observed that early age compressive strength of the concrete mixer designed with flyash had lower strength in comparison to control mixes. This trend of reduced compressive in high volume fly ash concrete mix continued up to an age of 28days. However, at extended ages i.e. 56 days and 90 days, it can be noticed that high volume fly ash concrete mixtures designed at water-binder ratio of 0.40, compressive strength of the concrete mixes designed with flyash content up to 35% is at par with the control mixes. However, at 0.6 water-binder ratio, compressive of high volume flyash concrete mixtures were not found to be encouraging. Concrete mixer designed with 50% fly ash content have significantly lower, compressive strength in comparison to control mixer at all ages. At later ages, gain in the compressive strength in high volume fly ash concrete mixes was observed. This is probably due to the densification of the microstructure resulting from the Pozzolanic Reaction. Pozzalanic reaction in case of fly ash concrete mixes involves reaction between reactive silica and alumina constituent of fly ash with the Portlandite. It is essential to have presence of Portlandite for the continuation of Pozzalanic reaction. Pozzolanic reaction in case of fly ash concrete mixes results in the formation of secondary CSH and sometimes CASH, if alumina is available that contributes towards later age strength (A rora et al., 2017; Ahmed et al., 2019; Du et al., 2021; Park and Choi, 2021, Chen et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2021, Sun et al., 2021 ). The test results of flexural strength indicate that at 7days, high volume flyash concrete mixes had lower flexure strength value in comparison to control mixer. At 28days and 56 days, flexural strength of high volume concrete mixer were found to be higher to equivalent w.r.t control mixes. It was also observed that with an increase in fly ash content (limited to 40%) a proportionate increase in the flexural strength value had been noticed.

question: How does magnesium hydroxide (Mg(OH)2) solution treatment of bamboo fibers improve the durability of bamboo fiber-reinforced concrete under wet-dry cycling conditions compared to untreated fibers or conventional concrete?
answer: Mg(OH)2 solution treatment effectively removes amorphous surface deposits such as lignin, hemicellulose, and wax, revealing the cell wall structure and significantly improving hydrophilicity. This enhances interfacial bonding with the cementitious matrix, resulting in significantly reduced decline rates of compressive and flexural strengths after 16 wet-dry cycles, thereby providing better deterioration resistance than untreated bamboo fiber-reinforced concrete or conventional concrete.
text:
Optimization of bamboo fiber interfacial properties via magnesium hydroxide solution treatment. The interfacial properties of bamboo fibers directly influence the mechanical strength and durability of concrete. 29,30 Experimental results indicate that untreated bamboo fibers exhibit significant lignin, hemicellulose, and wax deposits on their surfaces, leading to weak bonding with the cementitious matrix. 31 In contrast, Mg(OH)2 treatment effectively removes amorphous surface deposits from bamboo fibers, with a clearly visible cell wall structure and significantly improved hydrophilicity, thereby enhancing interfacial bonding with the cementitious matrix. This result is consistent with the findings of Chen et al., 32 who reported that alkaline treatment effectively removes hydrophobic substances from bamboo fibers and improves their adhesion to cement. However, previous studies 33-35 primarily focused on sodium hydroxide (NaOH) treatment, whereas this study is the first to systematically evaluate the effect of the Mg(OH)2 solution. The findings confirm that Mg(OH)2 treatment is equally effective in improving fiber-matrix bonding while avoiding potential fiber degradation issues associated with NaOH treatment.

Durability analysis of bamboo fiber-reinforced concrete. Durability is a critical factor in the engineering applications of bamboo fiber-reinforced concrete (BFRC). 36 The results of this study show that after 16 wet-dry cycles, conventional concrete exhibits the highest reduction in compressive and flexural strengths, whereas untreated bamboo fiber-reinforced concrete demonstrates only slight improvement. However, the best durability performance is observed in BFRC treated with magnesium hydroxide, where the decline rates of compressive and flexural strengths are significantly reduced. This finding indicates that proper fiber treatment can markedly enhance the deterioration resistance of concrete. The conclusion aligns with the study by Ahmad et al., 37,38 who found that alkali-treated natural fiber-reinforced composites exhibit lower performance degradation under hygrothermal cycling. However, previous research 39,40 mainly focused on short-term durability assessments, while this study extends the evaluation to longer wet-dry cycling periods. The results further verify the positive long-term durability effects of Mg(OH)2 solution treatment on bamboo fiber-reinforced concrete, providing more reliable data support for practical applications.

Research significance and engineering application prospects. This study not only investigates the effect of bamboo fiber content on the mechanical properties of concrete but also systematically analyzes the optimization of fiber interfacial properties and durability through magnesium hydroxide solution treatment. Compared to previous research, 41,42 the key innovations of this study include: experimental determination of the optimal bamboo fiber content range in concrete, preventing the strength reduction caused by an excessive fiber addition; systematic evaluation of the effect of Mg(OH)2 solution treatment on bamboo fibers and demonstration of its effectiveness in improving fiber hydrophilicity, interfacial bonding, and durability; and conduction of long-term wet-dry cycling tests to validate the durability of BFRC, providing more comprehensive evidence for its practical application.

question: How do the physical and chemical properties of palm kernel shell (PKS) and laterite contribute to the reduction in compressive strength of concrete when used as partial replacements for granite and sand, respectively?
answer: PKS reduces strength due to its lightweight, porous nature, lower density and strength compared to granite, and poor interfacial bond with cement paste, which weakens load transfer and promotes microcracking. Laterite reduces strength because its fine clayey particles interfere with cement hydration, reducing the formation of calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gel, while increased void content from both materials further compromises matrix compactness.
text:
Fig. 4 illustrates the 28-day compressive strength results for concrete mixes with varying laterite and PKS replacement levels across different water-cement (w/c) ratios. Compressive strength decreases with higher w/c ratios and increasing laterite and PKS content. For example, the control mix (0% laterite, 0% PKS) achieves compressive strengths of 52.0 MPa, 47.5 MPa, and 42.0 MPa for w/c ratios of 0.4, 0.45, and 0.60, respectively. At a 0.4 w/c ratio, strength decreases from 47.0 MPa at 10% PKS to 43.3 MPa at 30% PKS with 10% laterite, with similar trends at higher w/c ratios. This reduction is linked to increased porosity and lower matrix density caused by PKS and laterite incorporation. PKS, being a lightweight and porous material, has a lower density and strength than conventional granite, while its poor interfacial bond with cement paste weakens load transfer and promotes microcracking. Laterite, with its fine clayey particles, interferes with cement hydration, reducing the formation of calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gel, which is crucial for strength development. Additionally, the increased void content at higher replacement levels further compromises matrix compactness, leading to strength reductions. Consequently, the control mix consistently outperforms laterite- and PKS-modified mixes, aligning with studies documenting the weakening effects of these alternative aggregates in concrete [34, 43, 44].

The interplay between compressive strength, void content, and initial surface absorption (ISAT 10) in the concrete reveals critical insights ( Figs. 5 and 6 ). The introduction of laterite and PKS as partial replacements for sand and granite, respectively, modifies concrete properties by reducing compressive strength while increasing void content and surface absorption, particularly at higher water-cement ratios. These changes are primarily attributed to the porous nature of laterite and PKS, their finer particles, and PKS's irregular shape, which collectively increase porosity and weaken the concrete matrix. Consequently, the use of these alternative materials necessitates careful consideration in mix design to achieve a balance between strength and durability, particularly in structural applications.

question: Why is the influence of surface treatment on the tensile strength of lightweight foamed concrete most effective at an intermediate specific gravity of 1.2?
answer: The effectiveness is attributed to an optimal balance between matrix density and aggregate-paste interaction. At lower densities, the weak matrix limits strength, whereas at higher densities, the enhanced matrix properties overshadow the benefits of surface treatment.
text:
The influence of surface treatment on tensile strength development appears most effective at intermediate density levels (s.g. 1.2), where the balance between matrix density and aggregatepaste interaction reaches an optimal point. This phenomenon could be attributed to the competing effects of matrix densification and interfacial bond strength. At lower densities, the relatively weak matrix limits overall strength development, while at higher densities, the enhanced matrix properties begin to overshadow the benefits of surface treatment.

Cement content consistently emerges as a critical factor in strength development across all s.g. levels. The relationship between cement:OPKS

ratio and tensile strength demonstrates a generally linear trend, with higher cement content contributing to improved strength values. This correlation becomes more pronounced at higher s.g., suggesting synergistic effects between matrix density and binder content. The 3.3:1 cement:OPKS ratio consistently produces the highest strength values within each density category, indicating an optimal balance between aggregate content and paste volume.

The comprehensive analysis of tensile strength development provides valuable insights for material optimization in practical applications. For non-structural applications requiring moderate strength, compositions with s.g. 1.2 and surface-treated aggregates offer an optimal balance between performance and material effi - ciency. Applications demanding higher strength capabilities would benefit from compositions with s.g. 1.4, particularly when incorporating surface-treated aggregates and higher cement content. These findings have significant implications for the development of lightweight construction materials, particularly in seismic-prone regions where the combination of reduced mass and adequate tensile strength is crucial. The demonstrated improvements in tensile strength through surface treatment and optimal mix proportioning provide a foundation for developing more efficient and sustainable construction materials utilizing agricultural waste products.

Meanwhile, pozzolanic reactions from recycled fines may densify microcracks, enhancing long-term durability 47 . The results indicate that using ceramic waste as recycled aggregate in geopolymer concrete achieves higher compressive strength than recycled concrete aggregate. This is attributed to the stable mineralogical composition of ceramic material and its rough surface, which enhances bonding with the geopolymer matrix and its chemical stability in alkaline environments. question: What are the primary reasons attributed to the reduction in compressive strength observed in concrete mixes with 15% sugarcane bagasse ash (SCBA) replacement compared to mixes with up to 10% replacement?
answer: The reduction in compressive strength at 15% SCBA replacement is attributed to the decrease in the amount of ordinary Portland cement (OPC) and the higher porosity nature of the SCBA. Additionally, the low reactivity of SiO2, decreased CaO contents, and slow hydration reaction contribute to the reduced strength.
text: Figure 5 displays the results of compressive strength obtained for the Control Mix and SCBA-based samples (SCBA-P05, SCBA-P10, and SCBA-P15) after 14, 28, and 56 days of curing. To ensure data reliability and validate the observed trends, each experimental result represents the mean value of three measurements. Standard deviations (SD) were calculated for all compressive strength tests at 14, 28, and 56 days. The experimental test results revealed that the concrete mixes, at all percentages SCBA replacements 5%, 10%, and 15%, displayed a noticeably better compressive strength than the CM at all curing ages. It can be observed that the CS development is higher for the SCBA replacement up to 10% and reduced with an increase in the SCBA of 15%. The increase in CS with the incorporation of SCBA up to 10% could pertain to a high percentage of silica reacting with calcium hydroxide and water resulting in CSH gel 68 . The reduction for the 15% SCBA may be due to the decrease in the amount of OPC and the higher porosity nature of the SCBA 69 . Furthermore, the low reactivity of SiO 2 , decrease in CaO contents and slow hydration reaction also tend to reduce the CS 32 . However, the findings revealed that CS increases for the SCBA-P-05, SCBA-P10, and SCBA-P15 SCBA substitution compared with CM at 28 days, respectively. The improvement in compressive strength is attributed to the high pozzolanic reaction and high amount of amorphous silica. Although, the substitution of up to 15% of SCBA still enhances the high strength of concrete in comparison to CM. The addition of SCBA certainly produces comparatively high-strength concrete because of its finer particles, high silica content, and improved surface area resulting in number of nucleation sites for further hydration products 31 . The increase in the CS for SCBA-P05, SCBA-P10, and SCBA-P15% mixes compared to CM was 17.74%, 18.71%, and 3.87%, at 28 days, respectively. For instance, on 14 and 28 days, the SCBA-P05 sample strength was higher compared to CM by 11.69% and 17.74% respectively for the age of 14 and 28 days. Similarly, the CS of the SCBA-P10 concrete was greater than the CM by 13.42% and 18.71%, respectively. The same trend was followed by SCBA-P15 with an increase of 1.73% and 3.87% on 14 and 28 days, respectively, slightly larger than the CM. Additionally, the increase in CS development from 14 days to 28 days was remarkably higher for SCBA-P10 compared to SCBA-P05. The results also showed that at 56 days of age, the strength increase for the SCBA-P05, SCBA-P10, and SCBA-P15 samples were 12.28%, 14.29%, and 1.75%, respectively, higher than CM. The low early CS and enhanced later-age CS are common characteristics of pozzolans, such as SCBA 32,69 . The CS results indicated that 10% of SCBA is an optimal limit for replacement of OPC.

question: What are the three clearly defined zones in the typical load-displacement response of a tubular composite material subjected to quasi-static compression, and how is the second region determined?
answer: The three zones are the pre-crushing zone, the crushing process region, and the compaction zone. The pre-crushing zone spans from the starting point to the maximum crushing force, while the subsequent region after the crushing process is determined by the average load applied during crushing.
text:

Using the Instron 600 DX0 universal testing system with a full load range of 100 KN, as shown in Figure 6, a static axial compression load will be used in this investigation. The load plates will be adjusted to be parallel to one another prior to the test. Every specimen, which was composed of two fiber layers, will be subjected to three tests. Every stage of the crushing test for every specimen will be recorded on camera in order to record any potential failure mechanisms and ensure that all testing has been completed. Furthermore, the load and displacement parameters will continually monitor using an automated data collection system. This comprehensive approach ensured that all aspects of the specimen's behavior under compressive loading will be documented, from the initial stages of deformation to final failure. The combination of video recordings and automated data acquisition allowed for a thorough analysis of the mechanical response of the specimens, ensuring accurate characterization of their performance during the crushing tests. Thus, the best result of the three tests will be provided during the findings of this study, it is noteworthy that the results were consistently reproducible.

The region can be partitioned into three clearly defined zones. The first section, referred to as the pre - crushing zone, spans from the starting point to the maximum crushing force. The subsequent region after the crushing process is determined by the average load applied during crushing. The third zone is commonly known as the compaction zone. Microscopic investigations of composite tubes provide crucial insights into their microstructure and properties. question: What does the inverse correlation between compressive strength and water absorption in oil palm shell lightweight concrete, with an R-square value of 0.67 under NW curing conditions, indicate about the relationship between these two properties?
answer: It indicates a significant link where higher compressive strength generally results in lower water absorption, which enhances the concrete's overall durability.
text:

This higher absorption is likely due to the inherent porosity of untreated OPS, which allows more water to penetrate. In contrast, specimens treated with styrene acrylic emulsion (SAE) show significantly lower water absorption rates. The treatment effectively reduces porosity by filling voids and improving the density of the concrete matrix, leading to lower permeability and enhanced durability.

The comparison of curing conditions reveals that NW curing consistently yields the lowest water absorption rates over time, reflecting the optimal hydration environment provided by continuous water exposure. Conversely, AC and EC conditions show less reduction in water absorption, with specimens often exhibiting higher rates compared to those cured under NW conditions. This difference underscores the importance of maintaining moist curing conditions to achieve the best performance in terms of water absorption.

Notably, certain specimens, such as ST20 and ST25, exhibit increased water absorption after 56 days under NW curing conditions. This anomaly may be attributed to excessive SAE, which can lead to the formation of voids if not properly balanced. The inconsistency in water absorption for these specimens suggests that while SAE treatment is beneficial, its concentration must be carefully controlled to avoid adverse effects.

The relationship between compressive strength and water absorption of OPS lightweight concrete was analyzed using regression models, as shown in Figure 7. The analysis identified a notable inverse correlation: as the compressive strength increases, the water absorption rate decreases. This correlation was strongest in specimens cured under NW conditions, with an R-square value of 0.67, indicating a significant link between the two properties. The observed trend was consistent across all curing environments, including alternative and open curing, highlighting that higher compressive strength generally results in lower water absorption, enhancing the concrete's overall durability.

question: How does the total cumulative energy dissipation of a GFRP-reinforced conventional concrete slab compare to that of a steel-reinforced concrete slab, and what advantages are cited for GFRP regarding ultimate load-carrying capacity?
answer: The GFRP-reinforced slab exhibited a total cumulative energy dissipation of 48.4 kN·mm, which is higher than the 32.58 kN·mm recorded for the steel-reinforced slab. GFRP is cited as a viable alternative for applications requiring higher ultimate load-carrying capacity due to its corrosion resistance, light weight, high strength-to-weight ratio, non-magnetic and non-conductive properties, and durability.
text:
For the steel-reinforced concrete slab, the maximum load recorded was 15 kN, accompanied by the corresponding maximum lateral displacement of 6 mm. The initial stiffness of the slab was 5.0 kN/mm, and it is evident that the stiffness continuously degraded throughout all cycles. After 5 cycles, the stiffness was reduced from 5 kN/mm to 2.5 kN/mm. In contrast, energy dissipation increased with each subsequent cycle. After 5 cycles, the energy dissipation increased from 0.4 kN·mm to 16 kN·mm. The total cumulative energy dissipation was 32.58 kN·mm.

For the GFRP-reinforced conventional concrete slab, the maximum load recorded was 16.5 kN, with the corresponding maximum lateral displacement of 7.3 mm. The initial stiffness of the slab was 5.45 kN/mm, and it is clear that the stiffness progressively degraded throughout all cycles. After 6 cycles, the stiffness decreased from 5.45 kN/mm to 2.26 kN/mm. On the other hand, energy dissipation increased with each successive cycle. After 6 cycles, energy dissipation increased from 0.37 kN·mm to 18.7 kN·mm, with the total cumulative energy dissipation reaching 48.4 kN·mm.

GFRP has several advantages that make it a viable alternative in specific applications requiring a higher ultimate load-carrying capacity compared to steel-reinforced slabs. These advantages include:

- Corrosion resistance: Unlike steel, GFRP does not corrode, making it highly suitable for structures exposed to harsh environmental conditions such as marine, industrial, or chemically aggressive environments.
- Light weight: GFRP is significantly lighter than steel, which reduces the overall dead load of a structure and facilitates easier handling, transportation, and installation.
- High strength-to-weight ratio: While the stiffness may be lower, GFRP offers a high tensile strength relative to its weight, making it efficient in specific structural applications.
- Non-magnetic and non-conductive: GFRP is ideal for structures where electromagnetic interference or electrical conductivity must be minimized, such as MRI rooms or power plants.
- Durability: GFRP's resistance to environmental degradation ensures long-term performance, reducing maintenance costs over the lifecycle of a structure.

question: What factors are identified as the main causes for the decline in density of laterite concrete samples as the lateritic soil content increases?
answer: The decline in density is mainly attributed to reduced particle density, higher porosity, increased water absorption, variable particle size distribution, aeration, air voids, and chemical interactions.
text:
Density is an important property of concrete that determines its mass per unit volume. the density of concrete can vary depending on the composition of its constituents and the specific mix design. Understanding the density properties of concrete is essential for various aspects, including structural design, load calculations, and material specifications. It allows engineers and contractors to assess the weight, mass, and performance characteristics of concrete in different applications. The densities of hardened concrete cube samples shown in Fig. 5 were found to range from 2345 to 2411 kg/m 3 which indicate concrete for structural and load bearing purposes and showed that the density decreases with increase in lateritic soil percentages in the concrete mix. The declining density of laterite concrete samples as lateritic soil content increases is mainly because of factors like reduced particle density, higher porosity, increased water absorption, variable particle size distribution, aeration, air voids, and chemical interactions. Overall, the unheated specimens possessed higher density properties than the heated samples though some of the results for unheated appear greater than normal weight concrete. This may be due to excess water from curing tank, since the samples were only surface dried before ­ weighing 69 .

## Compressive strength development

Compressive strength is a vital property of concrete that measures its ability to withstand compressive forces and is an important parameter for structural design and evaluation. The compressive strength development properties of concrete is essential for designing and assessing the durability performance of concrete structures. It helps in determining the appropriate curing conditions, evaluating the early-age strength gain, and ensuring the longterm durability and structural integrity of concrete ­ elements 70 . The development of compressive strengths for various unheated concrete mixes cured at 3, 7, 14, and 28 days respectively are presented in Fig. 6. The results show that compressive strengths increased with increase in the laterite content from at 3 days to 28 days curing with 18.51-26.55 N/mm 2 , 18.1-26.55 N/mm 2 , 20.20-28.4 N/mm 2 , 16.33-29.61 N/mm 2 , 20.91-32.65 N/mm 2 , and 20.34-32.80 N/mm 2 for control, 10% lat., 25% lat., 50% lat., 75% lat. and 90% lat. respectively. The results were generally higher than the control concrete, except for the mix with 10% laterite, which was marginally less than the control. These results appear to contradict earlier findings by Ukpata et al. 3 , where compressive strengths were found to increase with decrease in laterite contents. This may be attributed to the difference in the quality of lateritic sand used in the study.

question: Why does the unconfined compressive strength (UCS) of marine clay stabilized with a combined POFA-lime-CS system decrease when the calcined shale (CS) content exceeds 10%?
answer: Increasing CS beyond the optimum level of 10% causes a reduction in UCS because excess CS particles are not effectively bonded within the stabilized matrix, leading to weak zones, increased brittleness, and premature failure.
text:
In general, the treated specimens exhibited higher peak stress compared with the untreated marine clay, confirming the effectiveness of the combined POFA-lime-CS stabilization system. The improvement in UCS can be attributed to the combined effects of lime hydration, pozzolanic reactions, and the filler effect of CS, which promoted particle bonding and produced a denser soil matrix. The secondary pozzolanic reaction occurs between CaO from lime and silica or alumina from CS or POFA, leading to the formation of cementitious compounds (CSH and CAH) that enhance soil particle binding, as supported by the FESEM and EDX results shown in Figure 18b and Table 9 in the next sections.

At 7 days, the strength gain was mainly associated with early lime reactions, as shown in Figures 10 to 12. The inclusion of CS improved the stress resistance up to an optimum content, particularly at 10% CS, where the highest UCS was observed. This indicates that moderate CS content contributed to better particle packing and enhanced interlocking within the soil matrix. However, increasing CS beyond the optimum level caused a reduction in UCS, especially at 15% and 20% CS. This reduction may be related to excess CS particles that were not effectively bonded within the stabilized matrix, leading to weak zones, increased brittleness, and premature failure. With increasing curing time to 28 days, the stress-strain curves showed a clear increase in peak stress, indicating progressive strength development. This behavior is mainly due to ongoing pozzolanic reactions between the silica and alumina from POFA and calcium supplied by lime. The 10% CS mixture again showed the most favorable performance, suggesting that this content provided the best balance between filler effect and cementitious bonding.

The strength behavior became more dependent on the availability of lime and the proportion of CS for 90 curing days. In mixtures with adequate lime content, continued curing allowed further formation of cementitious products, improving the stiffness and peak strength. The distinct reduction in stress after the peak value observed in several treated samples indicates a significant modification from the ductile behavior of natural marine clay to a more brittle response following stabilization. Janani et al. [51] and Adekitan & Popoola [52] similarly reported that increasing pozzolana content and curing duration led to enhanced strength development. Harichane et al. [53] found that natural pozzolanalime combinations yielded higher strengths compared to lime or pozzolana alone, indicating that natural pozzolana alone is insufficient for soil stabilization.

question: According to Gutarowska, how do the primary metabolic activities of moulds differ when growing on organic building materials compared to inorganic building materials, and what is the consequence for inorganic materials?
answer: On organic materials with available carbon and optimum pH, moulds principally produce mycelium and extracellular enzymes, whereas on inorganic materials where mycelium growth is impeded, they increase the production of organic acids, which may cause microbial corrosion.
text:
The starch and casein-based glues used to ad - here wallpaper and cardboard to plaster are also degraded by extracellular enzymes and can pro - vide a carbon source for moulds [43]. De La Torre and Gomez-Alarcon [44] showed that moulds grew much slower in the medium containing mortar, reaching 60% less mycelial biomass and the amount of mycelial components chitin, glu - can, ergosterol decreased by 13-41%. This is evi - dence of the presence in the mortar of a factor that inhibits mould growth, such as high pH, but also the presence of chemical compounds that inhib - it the synthesis of cellular components (CaSO 4 , oxides of Ca, Al, Si, Fe, Mg, K, Na, S, possibly biocides). The presence of inorganic compounds from the mortar in the medium also significantly inhibited the production of extracellular enzymes. This may have been due to the initial pH of the medium, particularly mortar (pH = 10.2), which reduced the activity of most enzymes. The high pH of the mortar probably directed the mould me - tabolism towards the production of organic acids. The organic acids produced by Penicillium, Aspergillus and Trichoderma moulds are highly cor - rosive [44, 45]. Gutarowska [40] presented differ - ences in the production of enzymes and organic acids by moulds when growing on media with the addition of building materials of organic and inorganic origin indicate two mechanisms of ac - tivity of moulds in the biodeterioration of build - ing materials. Having an available carbon source and optimum pH, on organic materials moulds produce principally mycelium and extracellular enzymes, while on inorganic materials, where mycelium growth is impeded, they increase pro - duction of organic acids. Organic acids produced in oligotrophic conditions by moulds may be the reason for microbial corrosion on inorganic building materials [40].
